whyItExists.problem: A page has dozens of elements. You need to style some headings differently from others, or style links only inside the navigation, or change a button's look when the user hovers it.
whyItExists.solution: CSS selectors let you target elements with surgical precision — by tag, class, ID, attribute, relationship to other elements, or interaction state.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Every CSS rule starts with a selector. Use the most specific selector that correctly describes your intent.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Avoid overly complex selectors (deep descendant chains). They are slow to read and brittle — one HTML change breaks the rule.

explainModes.beginner: A selector is how you tell CSS which element to dress up. You can say 'all paragraphs', 'anything with the class card', or 'only the element with ID hero'.
explainModes.simple: CSS has many selector types: element (p), class (.card), ID (#hero), attribute ([type='text']), pseudo-class (:hover), and combinators (nav a). You can combine them for precision.
explainModes.standard: CSS selectors follow a specificity hierarchy: IDs beat classes, classes beat element selectors. Pseudo-classes like :hover, :focus, and :nth-child() match elements in specific states or positions. Combinators (descendant space, child >, sibling +, ~) express relationships between elements.
explainModes.technical: The Selectors Level 4 specification introduces :is(), :where(), :not() with complex arguments, and :has(). :is() and :not() inherit the specificity of their most specific argument. :where() always has zero specificity. :has() is a relational pseudo-class — it selects a parent based on its children.
explainModes.deepDive: Browser selector matching runs right-to-left for performance. In div.card p, the browser first finds all p elements, then filters those inside .card, then inside div. Writing rightmost selectors that are unique (p.lead rather than just p) reduces the match set early. The CSS Selectors Level 4 :has() pseudo-class enables parent selection, previously impossible in CSS, and is now supported in all major browsers.

content.text: Prefer class selectors over ID selectors for styling. IDs are unique — classes are reusable and have lower specificity, making them easier to override.

questions.question: Which selector targets all elements with class="btn"?
questions.explanation: Class selectors use a dot prefix: .btn targets all elements with class="btn".

questions.question: Which combinator selects only DIRECT children?
questions.explanation: The child combinator > selects only direct children. A B (space) would match any descendant at any depth.

questions.question: The :hover pseudo-class applies styles when an element has keyboard focus.
questions.explanation: :hover applies when the mouse cursor is over the element. :focus applies when the element has keyboard or click focus.

faq.q: When should I use an ID selector vs a class selector?
faq.a: Use IDs for JavaScript hooks or fragment links (#section). Use classes for all styling — classes are reusable and have lower specificity, making them easier to compose and override.

:nth-child(n) counts all siblings regardless of tag. :nth-of-type(n) counts only siblings of the same tag. li:nth-child(2) targets the second child only if it is an li; li:nth-of-type(2) always targets the second li.
:not(selector) applies styles to everything that does NOT match the selector. p:not(.lead) targets all paragraphs that don't have the lead class.
